children: By John McCormick and Anthony DeBarros

Two years after handing Republicans control of Washington, voters in Tuesday's election expressed displeasure over President Trump's job performance while voicing angst about the cost of living and the nation's overall direction.

Results from a large national survey showed many Americans went to the polls in a sour mood and looked to the midterm election for change in Washington as Democrats appeared well-positioned to take control of the House and had a shot at flipping the Senate.

High fuel and food prices were a top voter concern, with roughly nine in 10 of the electorate saying the cost of living was a crucial or major factor in their thinking on how to vote for Congress, according to results from a poll of more than 79,000 registered voters for the Associated Press and all the major television and cable news networks.
Roughly six in 10 voters said they were very concerned about the cost of food, with a similar proportion registering that level of worry about the price of gasoline or diesel.

Ahead of the election, Trump cast the economy as being on solid ground. In the closing weeks of the campaign, he said "the golden age of America is upon us," called the economy strong and said "inflation is way down."
Voters disagreed and blamed him for higher prices, with close to two-thirds saying inflation was up more because of his policies.

The Voter Poll by SSRS has a margin of error of plus or minus 0.6 percentage point for the full national sample. The poll includes registered voters in all 50 states with interviews at voting locations, online and by telephone between Oct. 19 and Nov 3.

Roughly four in 10 voters said one of the reasons behind their U.S. House vote was to express opposition to Trump, while three-quarters said they feel dissatisfied or angry about the way things are going nationally.

Congress remains deeply unpopular, with almost half saying they strongly disapprove of the job it is doing. Roughly seven in 10 voters said the institution isn't doing enough to provide checks and balances on the president.

The survey showed both political parties were viewed skeptically by midterm voters, with nearly six in 10 having an unfavorable view of the Republican Party and a bit more than half seeing the Democratic Party that way.
Republicans currently control the Senate 53-47, and have a 219-214 edge in the House — including one independent who conferences with the GOP. There are two vacancies.
In the wake of a presidency that has proven lucrative to Trump's family, about six in 10 voters said they think the nation's leader gives priority to his own personal interests over the country's.
Nine in 10 voters said government corruption was a crucial or major factor in deciding their vote for the U.S. House.
Offered a list of six issues and asked to pick the one that is the most important for the nation, about four in 10 picked the economy, while about a third said the state of democracy.

Three-quarters of those surveyed said the economy isn't so good or poor. Only about two in 10 voters said inflation caused their family severe hardship in the past year, but nearly almost six in 10 said it had caused moderate hardship.

The war with Iran has been a major factor in driving fuel and fertilizer prices higher, and about six in 10 voters said the U.S. made the wrong decision in taking military action there. Roughly three-quarters said the war was a crucial or major factor for their vote.

Asked about Trump's tariff policies, almost two-thirds of voters said they have hurt the economy. While views of the economy were overwhelmingly negative, many voters felt more comfortable with their own finances. More than half said their own family situation was better or about the same as two years ago.

Following aggressive immigration enforcement actions that have resulted in disruptions and even the deaths of some Americans, including two high-profile shootings of Minneapolis residents in January, roughly six in 10 voters said they disapprove of how the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency is doing its job. About six in 10 voters said they were very or somewhat confident that the election was conducted fairly and accurately across the country, down from about three-quarters in an AP VoteCast national survey in 2024.
